France.title: No. 257  March 2020 The Impact of Oil Prices on the US Economy
France.summary:
Since the late 2000s, US oil production doubled from 5 million barrels per day (Mb/d) in 2008 to 11 Mb/d in 2018, largely due to unconventional drilling techniques like hydraulic fracturing. Natural gas production also increased from 12 Mb/d oil equivalent (Mboe/d) in 2008 to 17 Mboe/d in 2018. This growth reduced US oil energy dependence from 57% in 2008 to 11% in 2018 and improved the oil trade balance from –$386bn in 2008 to –$50bn in 2018. The US accounted for 13% of global oil production in 2018, up from 7% in 2008, and 21.5% of global natural gas production in 2015.

The breakeven price for American shale oil decreased from over $80 per barrel in 2010 to nearly $40 per barrel in early 2017. While historically negative, the impact of oil price increases on US GDP has become less clear-cut since 2010. Increases now positively affect investment in the hydrocarbon sector, countering negative effects on consumption. Estimated elasticities of US GDP to oil prices after less than a year now range between –0.124 and +0.017.

France.title: Impact of the oil price decline on France and the global economy
France.summary:
Since mid-2014, oil prices have plummeted by over 70%, falling from above USD 100 per barrel to below USD 80 by October 2014, and reaching a latest data point of $28 on March 28, 2016. This decline is attributed to abundant supply, with North American unconventional oil production rising from 5 to 9 million barrels per day (Mb/d) in five years, reaching a 44-year high in spring 2015. OPEC has maintained production at over 32 Mb/d, increasing by about 1 Mb/d between 2014 and 2015. Iran's production, currently 3.2 Mb/d (40% exported to China), is expected to increase to 3.8 Mb/d by 2017 following the lifting of sanctions. The IEA forecasts US crude oil production to fall to 8.8 Mb/d in 2016 from a record 9.4 Mb/d in 2015, and does not foresee market rebalancing until early 2017. Global oil demand growth is projected to slow from +1.6 Mb/d in 2015 (totaling 94.4 Mb/d) to +1.2 Mb/d in 2016 (totaling 95.6 Mb/d).

The oil price decline is expected to add 0.1 point to France's GDP in 2016 and 0.15 point in 2017. However, benefits are limited by factors such as businesses rebuilding margins rather than investing or cutting prices, and households allocating savings to debt reduction. Oil-exporting countries face significant challenges; Russia's ruble depreciated 55% against the USD in 2014-2015, and its budget deficit reached 3% of GDP in 2015 despite a 10% spending cut. Saudi Arabia's foreign exchange reserves are being used to finance an 8% of GDP current account deficit in 2015. Venezuela raised pump prices for the first time since the 1990s to address a 24% of GDP public deficit. Investments and capital expenditure in the oil and gas sector contracted by 20% in 2015, with a more pronounced decline expected in 2016.

Chatham House.title: Why the current sanctions regime is failing, and how to fix it Volodymyr Dubrovskiy and James Nixey
Chatham House.summary:
The current international sanctions regime against Russia, including the oil-price cap imposed by the G7, EU, and Australia in December 2022, has failed to sufficiently target Russia's fiscal balance and reduce its ability to wage war. An earlier embargo on Russian oil exports in late 2022 inadvertently led to a spike in global oil prices, enabling Russia to earn record-high export revenues. Russia has circumvented the $60 per barrel oil-price cap by utilizing a "shadow fleet" of ageing tankers, falsifying insurance paperwork, misreporting prices, and engaging in transfer pricing.

To increase pressure on Russia, a modified oil-price cap should allow unlimited volumes of Russian oil exports but at rigorously enforced price discounts. This requires additional enforcement resources, physical interventions against "shadow fleet" tankers, tightening prohibitions on uninsured ships, and establishing a "white list" of reputable, non-Russian buyers. The price cap should be set using the 'cost, insurance and freight' (CIF) price instead of the current 'free on board' (FOB) price to deter transfer pricing. Even if the Trump administration reduces support for sanctions after August 2025, European countries could still rigorously enforce a modified cap due to their dominance in marine reinsurance and control of the Baltic Sea straits, through which 60% of Russia's seaborne oil exports travel.

all_summaries.title: Impact of the oil price decline on France and the global economy
all_summaries.summary:
Since mid-2014, oil prices have plummeted by over 70%, falling from above USD 100 per barrel to below USD 80 by October 2014, and reaching a latest data point of $28 on March 28, 2016. This decline is attributed to abundant supply, with North American unconventional oil production rising from 5 to 9 million barrels per day (Mb/d) in five years, reaching a 44-year high in spring 2015. OPEC has maintained production at over 32 Mb/d, increasing by about 1 Mb/d between 2014 and 2015. Iran's production, currently 3.2 Mb/d (40% exported to China), is expected to increase to 3.8 Mb/d by 2017 following the lifting of sanctions. The IEA forecasts US crude oil production to fall to 8.8 Mb/d in 2016 from a record 9.4 Mb/d in 2015, and does not foresee market rebalancing until early 2017. Global oil demand growth is projected to slow from +1.6 Mb/d in 2015 (totaling 94.4 Mb/d) to +1.2 Mb/d in 2016 (totaling 95.6 Mb/d).

The oil price decline is expected to add 0.1 point to France's GDP in 2016 and 0.15 point in 2017. However, benefits are limited by factors such as businesses rebuilding margins rather than investing or cutting prices, and households allocating savings to debt reduction. Oil-exporting countries face significant challenges; Russia's ruble depreciated 55% against the USD in 2014-2015, and its budget deficit reached 3% of GDP in 2015 despite a 10% spending cut. Saudi Arabia's foreign exchange reserves are being used to finance an 8% of GDP current account deficit in 2015. Venezuela raised pump prices for the first time since the 1990s to address a 24% of GDP public deficit. Investments and capital expenditure in the oil and gas sector contracted by 20% in 2015, with a more pronounced decline expected in 2016.

all_summaries.title: Why the current sanctions regime is failing, and how to fix it Volodymyr Dubrovskiy and James Nixey
all_summaries.summary:
The current international sanctions regime against Russia, including the oil-price cap imposed by the G7, EU, and Australia in December 2022, has failed to sufficiently target Russia's fiscal balance and reduce its ability to wage war. An earlier embargo on Russian oil exports in late 2022 inadvertently led to a spike in global oil prices, enabling Russia to earn record-high export revenues. Russia has circumvented the $60 per barrel oil-price cap by utilizing a "shadow fleet" of ageing tankers, falsifying insurance paperwork, misreporting prices, and engaging in transfer pricing.

To increase pressure on Russia, a modified oil-price cap should allow unlimited volumes of Russian oil exports but at rigorously enforced price discounts. This requires additional enforcement resources, physical interventions against "shadow fleet" tankers, tightening prohibitions on uninsured ships, and establishing a "white list" of reputable, non-Russian buyers. The price cap should be set using the 'cost, insurance and freight' (CIF) price instead of the current 'free on board' (FOB) price to deter transfer pricing. Even if the Trump administration reduces support for sanctions after August 2025, European countries could still rigorously enforce a modified cap due to their dominance in marine reinsurance and control of the Baltic Sea straits, through which 60% of Russia's seaborne oil exports travel.
